A Safe Town? Ostensible State or County Racial Climate Impacts Perceptions of Town-Level Racial Identity-Safety Cues
articles.abstract: Identity-safety cues (ISCs) are environmental signals that indicate one’s marginalized identity is valued. ISC contextual information may impact town evaluations. Over three experiments ( N = 1,107), we examine how single or multiple ISCs posted across storefronts (i.e., Black lives matter flag, Study 1–3) and the racial climate surrounding a hypothetical town (Study 2–3) impact attributions of ISC motives and town evaluations. Racial minorities and Black Americans perceived greater external diversity motives (e.g., social pressure) of a storefront with an ISC when all other storefronts had an ISC compared to when no other storefronts had an ISC (Study 1–3). Ostensible state- and county-level racially egalitarian climates elicited greater expectations of internal diversity motives and positive town evaluations (e.g., greater progressive policies, quality of life, Black residents) compared to prejudicial racial climates and towns with a single ISC (Study 2–3). Findings demonstrate the need to consider multiple levels of ISCs.

articles.title: Grateful for What and Whom? How Gratitude List Content Varies and Is Associated With Affective Responses
articles.abstract: A gratitude list activity, whereby one recalls and writes down things they are grateful for, is a well-studied intervention known to confer an immediate and even prolonged boost in well-being. However, the specific content people reflect on, and how it relates to affective evaluations and the impact of the intervention, remains underexplored. Using data from a global online study ( N = 19,265), we applied natural language processing to examine the content of gratitude lists, identifying 16 thematic clusters, with the most common one focused on social relationships. Next, we examined and found various sociodemographic and psychological differences in people’s gratitude list content. Further, mentioning themes related to family or nature was associated with greater increases in positivity following the activity. Overall, our findings highlight individual differences in what people naturally think of during this popular intervention and suggest opportunities for personalized modifications to enhance adherence to and effectiveness of the intervention.

articles.title: Implicit Prejudice Differentially Predicts Placement Into Valuable and Scarce Opportunities
articles.abstract: Racial excellence gaps persist, partly due to unequal participation in advanced learning opportunities. Guided by the opportunity hoarding framework, this research investigates whether White Americans’ pro-White/anti-Black prejudice differentially predict simulated Advanced Placement (AP) course admission decisions, and under what conditions—when the opportunity is valuable, scarce, or both. Across two experiments, we observed an unexpected overall pattern in which Black students were placed into higher priority tiers than White students. Nonetheless, greater implicit prejudice predicted larger White–Black differences in placement decisions, explained by placing Black students into lower tiers rather than White students into higher tiers. Critically, we found preliminary evidence that this pattern emerges only when AP participation was described as both valuable and scarce. Explicit prejudice showed less consistent associations with differences in placement decisions across studies. The valuable and scarce nature of advanced learning opportunities may amplify the effect of implicit prejudice in deciding who deserves access.

articles.title: Impressions of Deviant Disgust Expressions Are Functionally Specific
articles.abstract: How do people perceive those who violate emotional expression norms? Across four studies, impressions of people displaying disgust “inappropriately” depended on how the deviation occurred. Targets who failed to show disgust toward disgust-eliciting stimuli (“flat deviants”) were judged as less healthy and lower in social status. Conversely, targets who expressed disgust to neutral stimuli (“react deviants”) were judged as less open-minded and less cooperative. These impressions tracked inferred behavioral affordances: flat deviants were seen as more likely to engage in pathogen-risky behaviors, whereas react deviants were not. Consistent with these judgments, affective deviants were differentially “punished”: flat deviants were rated as less fit and less likely to be recommended for jobs emphasizing health and hygiene, whereas react deviants faced these penalties for jobs emphasizing cooperativeness. Thus, perceivers do not simply condemn emotional norm violations; instead, they draw on expression–environment mismatches to make functionally specific trait judgments and potentially discriminatory decisions.

articles.title: Is Authenticity Perceptible? Accuracy in Judgments of State Authenticity From Expressive Behavior
articles.abstract: Substantial research provides evidence that being perceived as authentic benefits well-being and relationships, but under-examined is whether perceptions of authenticity are accurate. Across five studies, we tested whether perceivers can accurately discern others’ state authenticity. In Studies 1 to 3, we investigated correspondence between perceived and felt authenticity within acquainted dyads. Romantic partners accurately discerned each other’s authenticity after making sacrifices (Study 1) and after discussing a topic of personal distress and desired partner change (Study 2). However, partners failed to accurately perceive each other’s felt authenticity when discussing relationship conflict (Study 3), possibly impacted by cognitive or motivational processes elicited by the relatively high interpersonal stakes at play in conflict. In Studies 4A and 4B, outside observers were sensitive to authenticity differences in participants from Study 3 when watching thin-slice videos of the conflict conversations. Overall, we discuss the importance of authenticity for impression formation and close relationships.

articles.title: Less Is More: Why and When Having Less Signals Competence
articles.abstract: Living with less has become increasingly popular in contemporary culture. It can simplify people’s lives and enhance their well-being. Beyond these intrapersonal benefits, we document a novel, interpersonal benefit of having less: individuals who own fewer possessions are perceived as more competent than those who own more. This effect arises because observers infer that they rely more on reasoning rather than feelings in decision-making. We further develop a three-condition descriptive model specifying that the effect emerges when having fewer possessions appears voluntary, when the possessions are primarily non-hedonic, and when the quantity of possessions is sufficient to meet minimum needs. This research extends the literature on the benefits of having less from an intrapersonal to an interpersonal perspective and identifies possession quantity as a new cue for perceived competence.

articles.title: Should I Stay or Should I Go? Preference for Consistency Predicts Choice Perseveration in the Monty Hall Problem
articles.abstract: Five incentivized studies ( N = 5,354) tested whether preference for consistency (PfC) predicts staying with one’s initial choice in the Monty Hall problem, despite the fact that switching maximizes the probability of winning. Studies 1 and 2 found that higher PfC predicts staying, even after controlling for need for closure, preference for structure, intolerance of uncertainty, conspiracy beliefs, and numerical competence. Studies 3 and 4 provided experimental evidence that incentives moderated the link between PfC and staying, but higher (vs. lower) PfC only attenuated rather than eliminated incentive sensitivity. Study 5 identified anticipated regret over switching and losing as a mechanism underlying the effect, showing that the link between PfC and staying held across cultural contexts, although its magnitude was culturally calibrated. Together, this research shows that consistency motivation governs choice perseverance in a task that is intentionally impersonal and assumed to be driven by probabilistic reasoning rather than motivational forces.

articles.title: Closing the Gap, Carrying the Burden: How Gender and Prosocial Motivation Shape Workplace Recognition
articles.abstract: Despite progress toward gender equity, women remain disadvantaged in gaining workplace recognition. We theorize that prosocial motivation helps women achieve parity in workplace recognition by providing a role‐congruent path to becoming valued advice sources. Drawing on social role theory and role congruity theory, we propose that women are less likely than men to occupy central positions in advice networks, but that high prosocial motivation closes this gap. Advice centrality, in turn, functions as a peer‐conferred signal of workplace recognition that supports leadership emergence and performance ratings. Across a time‐lagged, multi‐source field study and two online experiments, we find support for this model. Study 1 ( n = 275) shows that women occupy less central positions in advice networks than men, but that high prosocial motivation closes this gap. Advice network centrality further mediates the interactive effects of gender and prosocial motivation on leadership emergence and performance ratings. Two online experiments (Study 2a, n = 247; Study 2b, n = 248) provide converging causal evidence for these effects. These findings show that prosocial motivation helps women achieve parity with men in workplace recognition, while raising the possibility that such parity may rest on demands that fall asymmetrically on women.

articles.title: Inclusive Leadership as a Site of Struggle: Resistance and Mitigation Strategies for Sustaining Inclusion for Historically Marginalized Employees
articles.abstract: Scholars emphasize inclusive leadership's benefits for leaders and employees, yet existing theory largely overlooks the challenges leaders face when addressing disparities experienced by historically marginalized employees. Drawing on an inductive study of 47 historically marginalized STEM employees and 14 leaders they identified as inclusive, we model inclusive leadership as a three‐part process: (1) leaders’ inclusion efforts (attentive learning, talent amplification, and structural debiasing); (2) resistance to these efforts (skepticism, gatekeeping, fit critiques, and non‐compliance); and (3) leader strategies to mitigate resistance and protect inclusion (explaining value, co‐crafting strategies, evaluating fit critiques, and managing change momentum). We triangulate findings and test our theory's boundary conditions using qualitative data from three additional STEM samples: racial minority men, lower‐ranking women, and White males. The first two samples replicate our model; the third reveals that White men may perceive inclusive leadership differently than historically marginalized employees. By centering the perspectives of those most affected by bias, our study extends inclusive leadership theory. We offer a processual view that moves beyond detailing inclusive behaviors to highlight the challenges leaders face enacting them.

articles.title: Leaving on a High or Low Note? An Achievement Goal Perspective on Executive Retirement
articles.abstract: Executive retirement represents a pivotal career transition with significant implications. However, our understanding of the antecedents of executive retirement remains limited. We contend that, different from the retirement of general employees, it is important to position executive retirement within an achievement context and consider factors such as firm performance and achievement goal orientations. Drawing on late adulthood developmental psychology, we propose an achievement goal framework to theorize the relationship between firm performance and executive retirement, and the moderating roles of goal orientations. We theorize that firm performance is associated with two distinct mechanisms: the legacy fulfillment mechanism (salient for executives with high performance) and the selective prioritization mechanism (salient for executives with low performance), which together result in a U‐shaped relationship between firm performance and the likelihood of executive retirement. We further consider executives’ goal orientations as boundary conditions to probe the underlying mechanisms. We found general support for our theory using an archival dataset of 1840 chief executive officers from S&P 1500 firms (Study 1) and a two‐wave survey of 363 executives (Study 2). By integrating developmental psychology theories into the executive retirement literature, our research sheds light on executive retirement decisions through a developmental psychology lens.

articles.title: Personnel Psychology's 40 Questions Series: Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion in Organizations
articles.abstract: This article presents a curated set of 40 questions on diversity, equity, and inclusion in organizations (DEI) to address myths and misperceptions about its role in Industrial/Organizational (I/O) Psychology and Management research and practice. We crowdsourced questions from our professional networks and organized the responses into themes including foundations of DEI, the business case, DEI effectiveness, DEI resistance, legal interpretations, DEI pullback, measurement, and programs and vehicles. Though the review is not entirely comprehensive, the aim is to utilize the most up‐to‐date literature to answer many of the most pressing questions about DEI.

articles.title: The Bamboo Ceiling in the UK: Ethnicity–Gender Intersectionality, Risk Tolerance, and Leadership Attainment
articles.abstract: In the UK, Asians are often perceived as the “model minority” who face few hardships due to their strong educational performance and economic success. We question this perception by uncovering a “Bamboo Ceiling” in leadership attainment for certain Asian subgroups in the UK. Whereas many researchers and practitioners treat Asians as a monolith, we recognize heterogeneity among Asian subgroups and focus on comparing ethnic Chinese (the largest East Asian group) and ethnic Indians (the largest South Asian group). In Study 1, we analyzed CEOs and CFOs of the Financial Times Stock Exchange (FTSE) companies—the largest publicly listed companies in the UK—over a 14‐year period (2011–2024). There were virtually no ethnic Chinese CEOs or CFOs, whereas the representation of ethnic Indians in these positions did not differ significantly from that of Whites. In Study 2, we analyzed a large, nationwide dataset from the UK Biobank ( N = 322,734) to further investigate the moderating role of gender and the mediating role of risk tolerance. While ethnic Chinese overall experienced a Bamboo Ceiling (thus confirming Study 1's results), this main effect was moderated by gender: Ethnic Chinese men were significantly less likely than ethnic Indian and White men to attain leadership positions, a pattern partly mediated by ethnic differences in risk tolerance; by contrast, ethnic Chinese, Indian, and White women did not differ significantly and were each disadvantaged relative to their male counterparts. These effects were robust across survey‐based and polygenic measures of risk tolerance. Together, these findings underscore the importance of distinguishing among Asian subgroups and examining how ethnicity and gender intersect in leadership attainment.

articles.title: The Inclusion Hangover: A Daily Diary Study of the Reflective Mechanisms for Employee Well‐Being
articles.abstract: How included employees feel at work fluctuates meaningfully from day to day. Emerging research demonstrates that these fluctuations have important implications for employee well‐being. Yet little is known about the cognitive processes through which these effects extend beyond the workday. Drawing on Ilies and colleagues' (2024) model of work‐derived well‐being, we propose that evening work reflection constitutes a key mechanism linking daily perceptions of workgroup inclusion to next‐morning well‐being. We further argue that daily fluctuations in perceived workgroup inclusion carry greater psychological significance for employees who perceive themselves as underrepresented or non‐prototypical within their immediate work environment (i.e., contextual minorities), thereby exerting a stronger influence on subsequent work reflection and well‐being. Using a daily diary design with morning, afternoon, and evening surveys ( n = 3480 days; N = 389 employees), multilevel path analyses supported the proposed model, demonstrating that positive and negative evening work reflection explain how daily workgroup inclusion carries over to next‐morning well‐being. By identifying positive and negative work reflection as distinct pathways linking daily workgroup inclusion to employee well‐being, and establishing contextual minority status as a boundary condition of these processes, we advance understanding of how , and for whom , the effects of daily workgroup inclusion extend beyond the workday. Together, these findings underscore the importance of fostering day to day workgroup inclusion to support employee well‐being in increasingly diverse workplaces.

articles.title: Bias at Scale: Global Disparities in the Representativeness and Contextualization of Childhood Research
articles.abstract: Psychological science, including research on child cognition, behavior, and development, has traditionally relied on convenience samples drawn from a narrow range of sociocultural communities. Moving beyond the simplifying WEIRD/non-WEIRD dichotomy, this study estimates the global representativeness of children participating in developmental research across multiple metrics of human cultural experience. A systematic review of studies published between 2016 and 2020 in five leading journals reveals a disproportionate focus on children from communities situated at the extremes of all selected metrics. This bias is coupled with a selective disregard for cultural context in research originating from these overrepresented settings, reflecting a persistent double standard in how culture is treated across the field. Notably, studies involving children from underrepresented communities do not receive greater recognition (e.g., citations) unless they are embedded within larger, multinational research projects. We discuss the implications for representativeness, contextualization, and epistemic inclusion of these patterns, and we advocate for systemic change toward a genuinely global science of child development and psychological science more broadly.

articles.title: Depth or Breadth? Domain-Specific Expertise and Cross-Domain Engagement in the Development of Scholarly Excellence
articles.abstract: Scholarly excellence is often equated with deep specialization within a single domain, a premise embedded in doctoral training, peer review, and academic-evaluation systems. However, research from the emerging “science of science,” drawing on large-scale analyses of publications, citations, and career trajectories, suggests a more complex relationship between expertise, cross-domain engagement, and scholarly impact. This conceptual article synthesizes insights from the science of science, cognitive research on expertise, and organizational studies to examine the roles of domain-specific depth and different forms of cross-domain engagement in the development of scholarly excellence. We argue that depth and breadth are complementary capacities whose contributions vary across career stages and institutional contexts. We distinguish between multidisciplinary exposure, interdisciplinary integration, and, in rarer cases, transdisciplinary contributions that extend beyond existing boundaries. Domain-specific expertise supports technical mastery, credibility, and efficient knowledge accumulation, whereas integrative forms of cross-domain engagement facilitate recombination, problem reframing, and long-term intellectual influence. We further show how academic-reward structures favor depth while discounting integrative contributions. We conclude by outlining implications for doctoral education, faculty evaluation, and research policy, and by proposing a developmental framework that supports diverse trajectories of scholarly excellence.

articles.title: Extending Truth-Default Theory to Misinformation: Connecting Misinformation Scholarship and Deception Research
articles.abstract: This article connects deception research, specifically truth-default theory (TDT), to misinformation scholarship. Through TDT’s propositions and supporting empirics, we demonstrate how central questions in misinformation scholarship can benefit from deeper engagement with deception research and in particular TDT. Findings in the misinformation literature that have been surprising or unexpected (e.g., relatively few people are exposed to and share misinformation online) are predicted and explained by TDT. Robust conclusions from TDT about deception in human communication (e.g., people are truth-biased) are challenged by findings from misinformation research, prompting deeper investigation. Deception-detection research paradigms provide conceptual and empirical reference points relevant to the design of misinformation-detection tasks and interpretation of their results (e.g., true–false base rates, prompted vs. unprompted veracity judgments). Analytic approaches from TDT (e.g., analyzing accuracy for truthful and deceptive messages independently) support existing misinformation research aiming to understand the detection of misinformation and can holistically evaluate the outcomes of misinformation interventions, and TDT’s findings on how to improve deception-detection accuracy also suggest strategies for interventions that improve the detection of misinformation without undermining trust in credible news and information.

articles.title: Flow and Similar Attentional States in Autism and ADHD: A Scoping Review of Similarities and Differences
articles.abstract: Flow is a state of optimal engagement. Autistic individuals and individuals with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) might have variations in flow-like experiences, such as hyperfocus, autistic inertia, and monotropism, that diverge from traditional or typical definitions. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines, we systematically reviewed 43 publications, including empirical studies, reviews, and other literature, to examine these constructs. Results showed that attentional experiences associated with neurodivergence overlap with, but also differ notably from, typical flow. Autistic inertia hinders task initiation and transitions, in contrast to flow’s seamless engagement. Monotropism involves rigid, directed focus and repetitive, tenacious engagement, whereas flow allows for flexible adaptations to challenges. Hyperfocus is like flow regarding intense concentration and immersion but is often involuntary, lacks clear goals, and is associated with emotional dysregulation. Although commonalities exist across these attentional experiences, the greatest overlap occurs within autistic inertia, monotropism, and hyperfocus. Attention in autistic and ADHD individuals might be more dynamic than previously believed, with potential for transitions between these experiences. This fluidity can enhance focus and productivity but may also lead to negative outcomes, such as overly rigid fixation or difficulty engaging with and disengaging from tasks. Clarifying these differences and overlaps can inform tailored interventions and supports, helping neurodivergent individuals manage focus, reduce task-related stress, and optimize productivity.

articles.title: How Sexually Objectifying Others Undermines Connection and Collaboration
articles.abstract: Sexual objectification is widely recognized as a driver of gender inequality, harming women by reducing them to bodies and undermining their agency. Yet psychological science has rarely asked a consequential question: Does sexual objectification also harm the individuals who objectify? In this theoretical article, we reframe objectification as not only oppressive but also self-undermining. Drawing from social, cognitive, organizational, and relationship science, we argue that objectifying others can compromise the capacity to form close relationships, collaborate effectively, and function well in social and professional life. These costs are traced to four mechanisms—cognitive load, face–body attentional trade-off, goal-based perception, and dehumanization. These mechanisms are proposed to operate as parallel, mutually reinforcing pathways that converge on social miscalibration. The framework further motivates a methodological agenda for studying objectification as a dynamic, dyadic process embedded in ongoing interaction. By foregrounding the objectifiers’ costs, we extend existing theories and highlight objectification as a mode of social perception that degrades the very relationships and institutions on which objectifiers rely. Identifying these costs offers an additional reason to reduce objectification, one that complements rather than replaces concern for the harms it inflicts on targets.

articles.title: Inclusion That Excludes: Rethinking the Ecological Model for Mental Disability Through Defensive Dynamics, Institutional Power, and Capital Asymmetries
articles.abstract: This article offers a critical reworking of ecological and social-ecological models as applied to intellectual and developmental disabilities, autism, and severe mental illness. Drawing on a qualitative synthesis of 18 studies, we show that ecological frameworks are predominantly used as descriptive mapping devices, that power and inequalities enter analyses in partial and fragmented ways, and that intersystemic connections often generate formally inclusive yet experientially exclusionary arrangements. To address these limitations, we propose an Integrated Ecological Model for Mental Disability, which retains Bronfenbrenner’s multilevel architecture but introduces four structural extensions: asymmetry of reciprocity in the microsystem, the defensive mesosystem, capital-modulated exosystemic permeability, and the performative and normalizing exosystem. These concepts integrate Bourdieu’s theory of capital and field, Foucault’s genealogy of dispositifs , 1 and group psychoanalysis, and they are grounded in recurrent patterns observed across school transitions, family-service relations, residential services, and autism employment programs. The framework has implications for research designs that move beyond barriers and facilitators for multilevel clinical and educational interventions, and for normative debates on relational justice and psychopolitical validity in mental-disability policy.

articles.title: Moving on From Simple Operationalism: Anchoring Theoretical Constructs in Rich Relational Models
articles.abstract: Operational definitions have long been a core approach to measuring and relating observed data to theoretical constructs in psychological science. However, many contemporary modeling approaches conflict with the tacit assumptions of operationalism as it is implemented in psychology. Counterintuitively, these departures imbue model-based definitions of constructs with superior measurement properties, such as improved reliability and validity, when compared with their operationalizations based directly on observables. Instead of relying on operational definitions of constructs, we instead suggest that psychology should adopt relational definitions or relational operationalizations, representing constructs as latent variables in a multilevel generative model of behavior, self-report, or neuroimaging data. These model-based metrics can better reflect measurement error at multiple levels, account for the interactions between measurement devices (tasks, scales) and measurement objects (participants, processes), provide a holistic account of latent constructs and how they manifest across different measurements, facilitate convergence or discrimination tests among different tasks seeking to measure the same construct, and improve scientific communication by clarifying core psychological concepts. Relational definitions of important constructs should naturally emerge as researchers apply models more regularly, and these definitions and models will improve as researchers discover mathematical approaches that are suited to describing psychological processes.

articles.title: Searching for the Pattern: Understanding, Assessing, and Transforming Social Settings
articles.abstract: A historical analysis of systems theory ideas from the biological and physical sciences reveals their infusion into sociology and action-oriented subfields of psychology, including social, organizational, developmental, and community psychology. Constructs and processes are identified that are useful for creating a framework to understand, assess, and transform social settings. The central theoretical concept that surfaces is the emergent pattern of dynamic transactions that communicates critical information and meaning, referred to as “social regularity.” This is followed by an examination of the varying definitions and frameworks of proximal social settings (e.g., classrooms, community-based organizations, workplaces) in which individuals derive the bulk of their experiences in forming their character, identity, learning, and well-being. Social regularity is at the core of an evolving social-setting model that communicates meaning through several channels—control and power, modes of expressing communication, and the flow of information—that result in corresponding distributional equity outcomes. From these communication channels, an action model for transforming social settings to create more equitable aggregate-level individual outcomes and improved setting outcomes is explicated. Corresponding methods of measurement are described. Various strategies and tactics are suggested to directly target social regularities. Relational-, norm-, and structural-focused examples are provided.

articles.title: Social-Cognitive Frameworks for Understanding the Connection Between Social Isolation and Psychosis Risk
articles.abstract: Increasing evidence demonstrates an association between social isolation and psychosis risk. In this perspective, we attempt to account for why that is. Drawing from work in social psychology, social neuroscience, and clinical psychological science, we present two frameworks for understanding the association between social isolation and psychosis risk: the “social-needs” framework and the “social-processing” framework. Social needs states that because of people’s inherent social needs, isolation produces increased social attention, perception, and thought to fill the social void, resulting in the perception of anomalous social information and social meaning. Social processing states that the lack of exposure to social stimuli during isolation diminishes social processing (i.e., social thought, social perceptions) and may lead isolated individuals to turn their attention inward, blurring internal and external worlds and intensifying self-focus in a way that creates reality-monitoring disturbances and anomalous self-experiences. Conveniently, these frameworks can be empirically arbitrated. We review the literature connecting social isolation to psychosis, describe the frameworks, their empirical support, and the predictions they make, and discuss clinical implications. Ultimately, a better accounting of isolation’s pro-psychotic effects might lead to better efforts at psychosis prevention.

articles.title: The Developing Aesthetic Brain and Its Social Origins
articles.abstract: Neuroaesthetics has mapped the mature brain networks underlying aesthetic experience but lacks a developmental mechanism explaining how these networks become tuned to produce culturally specific preferences. The developmental-neuroaesthetics framework developed here centers on a two-system model: biological perceptual primitives (System A) and socially gated cultural tuning (System B). Cultural aesthetics are acquired through social gating during infancy, via mechanisms analogous to language acquisition. This process leverages infant-directed pedagogical signals and shared experience to flag culturally specific stimuli for affective learning. Neuroimaging evidence demonstrates that the infant medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) plays a specialized role in social perception from early in life, serving as the ontogenetic foundation for the adult mPFC’s aesthetic-valuation system. Interbrain synchrony during adult-infant interactions may provide a candidate mechanism through which shared experiences support aesthetic-value learning. The default mode network, of which the mPFC is a core component, is itself shaped by early social interaction, linking social experience directly to the neural substrate of aesthetic valuation. This framework reconciles cultural diversity with biological universals, generating testable predictions linking early social-neural responsivity to later cultural-aesthetic conformity.

articles.title: The Responsibility–Power–Justice Nexus: A Framework for Reorienting Behavioral Science Toward Power and Justice
articles.abstract: Behavioral science has achieved remarkable policy influence, yet the problems it addresses, such as climate change, health inequality, and financial precarity, have worsened. We argue this is no coincidence. The field suffers from systematic power-blindness: it treats individuals as abstract decision makers while bracketing the structural forces that shape their behavioral possibilities. This article develops the responsibility–power–justice (RPJ) nexus framework as a corrective, advancing two foundational claims. First, power is not external to behavior but constitutive of it; every behavioral intervention embeds claims about who bears responsibility for problems and solutions. Second, justice is not a normative standard applied after behavioral analysis, but a causal mechanism operating within it: Tax compliance depends on perceived fairness, health behaviors reflect institutional trust, and cooperation requires beliefs about equitable burden-sharing. Across climate policy, public health, and economic governance, we demonstrate a consistent pattern: powerful actors reframe structural problems as individual failures, behavioral science supplies the intellectual tool kit, and interventions redistribute responsibility downward while leaving power structures intact. We trace this pattern to the field’s roots in methodological individualism, its privileging of individual-level experiments, and its institutional entanglement with prevailing governance arrangements. We conclude by outlining what a justice-oriented behavioral science would require.

articles.title: Toward a Psychology of Science: A Dynamic Cognitive Model of the Evolution of Scientific Theories
articles.abstract: Responding to a recent call for the development of a psychology of science, we examine how scientists manage empirical anomalies, a routine yet consequential challenge in scientific practice, and how their responses shape theory development. We argue that defensive anomaly-reduction strategies, which allow researchers to preserve an initial theoretical claim, can generate important secondary benefits. During the emergence phase of a theory, they foster auxiliary revisions that may reduce underfitting and place a fragile theory on a growth trajectory. During the exploitation phase of established theories, they help sustain attention to problems derived from the theory and support cumulative research. However, their accumulation may also increase the risk of overfitting, reduce predictive power, and set the theory on a degenerative trajectory. We illustrate these dynamics primarily through examples drawn from psychological theories, with a focus on responses to replication failures. Last, we derive several implications for peer review aimed at fostering scientific innovation. In particular, we propose shifting evaluation away from the consistency of findings, which may penalize emerging research programs and hinder innovation, and toward how inconsistencies are managed, thereby fostering growth trajectories, including for mature programs confronted with anomalies.

articles.title: Two Practices That Understate the Mental Health Risks Associated With Adolescent Social-Media Use
articles.abstract: Why do researchers analyzing the same body of evidence reach different conclusions about whether social-media use poses risks to adolescent mental health? We offer a partial explanation: Two common practices can lead researchers to underestimate harm and reach divergent conclusions. First, studies often do not account for risk elevations, relying instead only on correlation coefficients, which are more prone to misinterpretation. Second, researchers often rely on highly blended analyses that combine heterogeneous exposures (e.g., multiple digital activities, including “TV watching”), outcomes (e.g., depression with life satisfaction), and populations (e.g., girls with boys), and then treat weak aggregate associations as evidence that specific risks are negligible. This is especially problematic when the central question is whether heavy social-media use is associated with internalizing symptoms among adolescent girls. We illustrate how sequential blending can transform a large and clinically relevant association into a negligible one, which helps explain the persistent disagreement in the literature. We conclude by urging researchers to present their findings in more practically interpretable terms, including elevated risks, and to investigate heterogeneity across platforms, usage levels, populations, and outcomes.

articles.title: What We Talk About When We Talk About Empathy: Toward a Common Lexicon of Empathy-Related Constructs
articles.abstract: Almost since the term “empathy” was coined, there has been scholarly disagreement about its meaning. Today it can best be viewed as an umbrella term encompassing a host of more specific constructs, almost all of which are regularly referred to as “empathy” in some form or fashion. Promiscuous use of this global label to denote very different constructs has impaired communication among and between scholars, practitioners, and the general public. A team of 15 empathy scholars assessed this issue and created a lexicon for these specific lower-order constructs. In this article we report the result of this effort. The lower-order constructs making up this lexicon are vicarious affect , emotional contagion , emotion co-sharing , sympathy / compassion , personal distress , perspective taking , accurate inference , mimicry , synchrony , projection , and transportation . We recommend that this more specific language be used more frequently and that the umbrella term “empathy” be used more sparingly.

articles.title: Carving stories at their natural joints.
articles.abstract: Over the past three decades, psychology has documented the recurrence of specific themes in stories across cultures (e.g., love, alliances, monsters, and imaginary worlds) and linked them to identifiable motivational mechanisms (e.g., mate choice, cooperation, threat detection, and exploration). Yet this body of work has remained fragmented, organized around individual themes rather than integrated into a unified account of what makes narrative content psychologically engaging. Here, we propose the Motivational-Ingredient Framework. We identify a set of motivational ingredients: core narrative features, each defined by the specific motivational mechanism it activates. Drawing on evolutionary psychology, affective neuroscience, and the study of human motivation, we compile a comprehensive table of ingredients grounded in the current understanding of human motivational architecture. This framework offers a theory-driven, cross-culturally applicable foundation for the empirical study of narrative content, with implications for fields ranging from media psychology and computational humanities to education and public policy. articles.title: Dynamics of variability and bias in working memory.
articles.abstract: Visual working memory performance declines with the quantity of material stored and the duration of its maintenance, but it is disputed whether these constraints are independent or interact. Specifically, different studies have reached contradictory conclusions on whether greater memory load accelerates deterioration of the stored information during retention, a question with implications for storage mechanisms. Meanwhile, prominent models of visual working memory based on stable attractors predict that recall should become increasingly biased toward a fixed set of canonical features with longer retention, but empirical support is mixed. Uncertainty is further exacerbated by limited data, methodological variation, and inconsistent analytical approaches across studies. Moreover, previous studies have not always distinguished response variability from stimulus-specific biases nor considered the possibility of swap errors (intrusions). To address these issues, we conducted six new experiments and reanalyzed data from seven published experiments using consistent analytical methods to examine the effects of set size and delay on variability and bias. Our results show that recall variability increased with longer delays and higher set sizes, consistent with prior findings, and importantly, that these effects did not operate independently: The effect of delay was amplified at higher set sizes. We also observed consistent evidence for systematic biases across stimuli, but unlike variability, bias amplitude did not change with either set size or retention interval. These results support diffusion accounts of visual working memory maintenance, in which variability grows through the accumulation of random error, while challenging stable attractor accounts that predict systematic drift toward canonical values during maintenance. articles.title: Idea generation during emotion regulation: A proposed framework.
articles.abstract: The field of emotion regulation (ER) is increasingly recognizing the influence of context on an individual's regulatory processes, prompting researchers to examine how specific circumstances dynamically shape ER. Well-accepted theoretical models and supporting empirical studies frame such situation-specific ER as a sequence of stages involving decision points: choosing to regulate, selecting a strategy, deciding whether to maintain current regulatory efforts, and so forth. These frameworks, however, omit an underappreciated process that we argue underscores ER at its highest specificity: idea generation. In other words, individuals do not just select properties of their regulatory attempt, but must actually generate an attempt-a distinction that leverages an underexplored level of analysis in ER known as techniques. In this article, we integrate multiple theoretical perspectives across domains to demonstrate the feasibility in (and insight afforded by) measuring idea generation in ER. Next, we review how existing empirical paradigms already utilize generation-related principles in largely unacknowledged manners, with some studies that have specifically targeted these generative operations during ER. We combine these observations into a novel framework called Emotion Regulation Generation of Techniques, which serves to deepen the study of ER by delineating a generation stage that follows and informs selection mechanisms. To help study idea generation in practice, this framework is equipped with methodological protocols that draw from neighboring domains (e.g., divergent thinking), paired with future directions and testable hypotheses that can inform the role of idea generation in healthy regulation and in dysregulated affective disorders. articles.title: Why most stereotypes are negative.
articles.abstract: Stereotypes are a foundational construct in psychological science, often defined as beliefs concerning characteristic group attributes. We present a cognitive-ecological theory of social perception that predicts and explains why such characteristic attributes are likely negative, that is, why most stereotypes are negative. The theory assumes that, cognitively, people characterize groups by attributes that distinguish them from other groups. Ecologically, positive social information is more frequent (i.e., positivity prevalence), and negative social information is more diverse (i.e., negativity diversity). If negative attributes are less frequent and more diverse relative to positive attributes, then they must be more likely to distinguish one group from another. Consequently, the attributes people see as characteristic of a group are likely to be negative. We illustrate the predicted stereotype negativity across two studies and two existing data sets. We then formalize the theory and illustrate it with simulations showing that rare attributes can be highly diagnostic of group membership while applying to only a minority of group members. Thus, the theory explains why most stereotype content is likely negative, despite the well-documented positivity prevalence, and why stereotypes may be diagnostic and comparatively accurate, despite being descriptively inaccurate. The theory explains stereotype negativity without requiring motivational derogation, essentialist group differences, or a general negativity bias, and it clarifies when positive stereotypes should occur. We also discuss the theory's relation to dimensional models of stereotype content and consequences for interventions aimed at reducing stereotype negativity. articles.title: Psychological Reactions to Subordinates’ LLM Use at Work
